package_info.why_malicious: The package exploited a process flaw in the Azure SDK release pipeline: by adding the 'azure-sdk' npm account as a collaborator, the Azure SDK bot automatically listed the package as an official release. This allowed the attacker to publish a package that appeared to be an official Microsoft Azure SDK, potentially deceiving users into installing it. While the code in this instance was a proof-of-concept, the same technique could be used to distribute malicious code under the guise of a trusted vendor.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Proof-of-concept code from Birsan's dependency confusion packages
console.log('This is not a dependency confusion test.');
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the package is imported, it prints a disclaimer message to the console. In the original dependency confusion proof-of-concept, similar code was used to demonstrate the ability to execute arbitrary code, and in real attacks, this could be replaced with code to exfiltrate environment variables or other sensitive data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The presence of proof-of-concept code that executes automatically upon import is highly unusual for an official SDK package. In similar attacks, this pattern has been used to run arbitrary code, including exfiltrating secrets or installing additional payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Official Azure SDK packages are expected to contain only production-ready, reviewed code. They should never include arbitrary code from external researchers or code that executes automatically for demonstration purposes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Test or demonstration packages may print messages to the console, but this is not appropriate in production SDKs, especially those distributed under an official vendor's name.
key_indicators: index.js file containing code that prints unexpected messages to the console
Automatic code execution on import in a package claiming to be an official SDK
Presence of proof-of-concept or test code in a package listed as an official release
No legitimate changelog or release notes explaining the presence of such code

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes a package to npm with a name similar to official Azure SDK packages.
Attacker adds the 'azure-sdk' npm account as a collaborator to the package.
Azure SDK bot automatically picks up any npm package where 'azure-sdk' is a collaborator and adds it to the official releases CSV.
The package appears on the official Azure SDK Latest Releases page, giving it legitimacy.
If the package contained malicious code, it could be installed by unsuspecting users, leading to code execution.

behavioral_signatures: Packages with names closely resembling official Azure SDK modules appearing in official SDK listings without prior announcement
Packages that add high-profile or organization accounts (such as 'azure-sdk') as collaborators without a legitimate project history
Unexpected console output or presence of proof-of-concept code in production SDKs, especially during import or installation
file_indicators: index.js containing code that prints messages unrelated to SDK functionality
Package metadata (package.json) listing 'azure-sdk' as a collaborator for packages not published by Microsoft or the official Azure SDK team
network_indicators: No direct network indicators in this proof-of-concept, but similar attacks may include code that exfiltrates data to attacker-controlled domains or IP addresses
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor official SDK listings for new packages not published by trusted maintainers. Audit collaborator lists for the addition of high-profile accounts to unknown or unvetted packages. Scan package contents for unexpected or proof-of-concept code, such as console output or code that executes automatically on import. Flag and review any package that appears in official listings but does not have a corresponding release announcement or changelog from the official team.
